messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 72

He walks into the office at 7:03 each morning, always three minutes late, always with a travel mug of black coffee that he never finishes. The security guard nods; he doesn’t nod back. By 9 a.m. he has logged into his work queue, forty-seven unresolved tickets blinking on his screen, and his shoulders are already tight. He works from a cubicle near the emergency exit — he picked it himself, first day on the job, told his manager he liked the natural light. The truth is he needs to know the way out.

He was twenty-two when he joined the army of his home country, a small Southeast Asian nation still fingering the scars of a decades-long civil war. His unit was sent to clear a village north of the capital, something about insurgent activity. He remembers the heat, the way the rice paddies shimmered like broken glass, and the smell — wet earth and something metallic. He was the radio operator, crouched behind a low wall, calling in coordinates when the mortars came. The first round hit fifty meters left. The second landed directly on the command post where his sergeant, a man named Chandara, had been standing. He saw Chandara’s torso separate from his legs, and he remembers thinking *that isn’t real*, even as the blood soaked into his own uniform.

He was the one who called the medevac. He still hears the radio static, his own voice cracking. For two weeks afterward he stayed on base, slept with his boots on, could not close his eyes without seeing the red mist. He was sent home with a commendation and a diagnosis no one used the words for. He never spoke about it. His family said he seemed “quiet.” His fiancée, now his wife, said he had changed. He said nothing.

Now he is forty-six. He works from a beige cubicle in a tech park outside Austin, writing code for a logistics platform. The work is good — repetitive, logical, predictable. He likes that. But he cannot sit with his back to a door. He has rearranged his desk so he can see the hallway. When a coworker claps him on the shoulder unexpectedly, his hand jerks and his heart hammers for thirty seconds. He has learned to say “Sorry, I’m just jumpy today.” He says it at least twice a week.

At home he is quieter still. His wife of twenty-three years has learned not to ask about the nightmares. She hears him thrash in the dark, sometimes shouting numbers — coordinates, she thinks — and she waits. In the morning he says nothing. He takes his coffee and drives to work with the windows up, scanning every intersection for something he cannot name. He avoids crowds. He avoids the news. He avoids the Vietnamese grocery store because the smell of fish sauce brings the rice paddies back. He has not visited his mother in ten years. She lives in Phnom Penh. He sends money, but he cannot explain why he will not come.

Last month his manager asked him to lead a team meeting in the glass-walled conference room. He said he had a dentist appointment. He went to the parking lot and sat in his car for an hour, sweating. He does not think of himself as broken. He thinks of himself as someone who learned to hold very still. The world has a high ceiling and he is always listening for a sound he cannot identify — a whistle, a hiss, the first whisper of an inbound round that never comes.
